extracted.intended_audience: University of Alaska (UA) system faculty and staff who may engage in federal lobbying or related activities
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for University of Alaska system employees on when activities count as lobbying under the federal Lobbying Disclosure Act (LDA), what must be registered/reported, which officials are "covered," what expenses count, and who to contact for compliance assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: LDA registration and quarterly reporting obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lobbying Disclosure Act (LDA) of 1995 (as amended in 2007) requires certain organizations to register as lobbying entities with the U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate and report quarterly on all lobbying activities and expenses. Based on the requirements outlined in the law, the University of Alaska (UA) system must comply with the registration and reporting obligations in the LDA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UA must follow the LDA's registration and quarterly reporting requirements; contact the Office of Government Relations for assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office of Government Relations is responsible for LDA compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of Government Relations, Federal Relations team in the UA System Office is tasked with compliance with the LDA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any LDA-related questions should be directed to John Latini (jalatini@alaska.edu), Executive Director of Federal Relations for the UA system. UA system employees are strongly encouraged to contact the Office of Government Relations, Federal Relations team before engaging in any lobbying activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty & staff must report lobbying when acting in official capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: ALL UA faculty and staff that engage in lobbying in their official capacity as UA system employees should report lobbying activities and expenses. Faculty and staff that contact, urge, or lobby federal officials in their personal or professional capacity do not have to report these activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Relations team sends quarterly emails requesting reporting of appropriate expenses and activities; if you are not receiving these emails, contact John Latini.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of lobbying activities (including Lobbying Contacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbying activities (including Lobbying Contacts) are defined as any oral, written, or electronic communication to a covered official regarding any aspect of federal legislation (including funding), rules, regulations, Executive Order, program, policy, confirmation, or position of the United States Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition includes any preparation or planning activities, research, and other background work intended to support lobbying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered legislative branch officials (who count as 'covered')
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered Legislative Branch Officials include: Members of Congress (House and Senate); Congressional staff; Congressional Committee staff; Joint Congressional Committee staff; Congressional working groups or Caucuses; and Officers in the House and Senate (e.g. Clerk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure whether an individual is a covered legislative official, contact John Latini for classification guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered executive branch officials (who count as 'covered')
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered Executive Branch Officials include: President of the United States; Vice President; Employees of the Executive Office of the President; Employees serving in a position in level I, II, III, IV, or V of the Executive Schedule; Members of the uniformed services whose pay grade is at or above O-7; and Employees serving in a position of a confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Executive Office of the President includes offices such as OSTP, Climate Policy Office, OMB, ONDCP, and the National Space Council; contact John Latini with classification questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule: Senate-confirmed officials are covered
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, any federal official subject to Senate confirmation will be a covered executive branch official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt about whether an official is covered, consult the Federal Relations team (John Latini).

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as lobbying expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbying expenses include travel costs, employee salaries, office overhead, and payments to vendors (including professional societies and organizations if university funds are used to pay for membership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting lobbying, include these categories of expenses as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting a Congressional letter of support is lobbying
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes, essentially all activities that request a Member of Congress or Congressional staff to take any action are considered lobbying activities and should be reported to John Latini.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty and staff are strongly encouraged to contact the Office of Government Relations, Federal Relations team to seek a Congressional letter of support for proposals submitted to federal agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contacting a federal program manager usually is not lobbying
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally speaking, no. Federal program managers are typically not considered covered officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a general rule; consult the Federal Relations team if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting a meeting with Congressional staff to secure funding is lobbying
rubrics_metrics.description: Emailed staff in an Alaska Member of Congress’ office to request a meeting to discuss securing federal funding for my work — this is considered a lobbying activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All aspects of such requests need to be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urging a Member to cosponsor a bill is lobbying
rubrics_metrics.description: If you saw an Alaska Member of Congress at an event and urged them to cosponsor a bill that would support your work, this is considered a lobbying activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All aspects of this engagement need to be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation in professional association visits is reportable only if acting for UA
rubrics_metrics.description: If you traveled with your professional association and visited Members of Congress to discuss the association’s legislative priorities, you do not need to report these engagements if you are not acting on behalf of the UA system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are acting on behalf of UA, the engagements would be reportable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of UA email or resources makes communication reportable
rubrics_metrics.description: Using my UA email address, I emailed an Alaska Member of Congress, or their staff, to urge the Member to protect funding or request funding be released for a federal program — this is considered a lobbying activity and needs to be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications made using university resources are reportable; contact Federal Relations for help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal communications using personal resources generally not reportable
rubrics_metrics.description: Using my personal email address to urge a Member of Congress or their staff is not considered a lobbying activity for LDA reporting because you reached out using personal resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You retain your First Amendment right to contact elected officials on your own time; such personal contacts are not subject to UA LDA reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference interactions and reporting details
rubrics_metrics.description: If at a conference you talked with a Member of Congress and/or their staff about the importance of your work including the need for federal investment, this is most likely reportable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may not need to report travel expenses for attending the conference, but you will need to report the topics discussed, provide your hourly rate, how long the engagement lasted, who you lobbied, and if other UA personnel participated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students are generally exempt from LDA obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: I had students join me in a meeting with a covered official on behalf of our program — do I need to report their time as well? No, in general LDA obligations do not apply to students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student participation is generally excluded; consult Federal Relations for edge cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campus tours: education vs lobbying distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Participating in or leading a campus tour that included covered officials where you educated the officials about your activities and described challenges (but did not request action) is not considered lobbying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you asked the covered official to take any actions (e.g., supporting increased federal funding), that would be considered lobbying and reportable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to get additional information and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: For questions contact John Latini (jalatini@alaska.edu), Executive Director of Federal Relations for the UA system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External resources: the U.S. House of Representatives’ Office of the Clerk maintains a Lobbying Disclosure website, and the U.S. Senate's Office of Public Records maintains a public disclosure website with LDA-related information.
